# Workshop 11
 
 # Deliberating with the Public: Democratic Engagement Series Wrap-Up
 
 **Speakers:** [Audrey Tang](https:/www.linkedin.com/in/tangaudrey/?locale=zh_TW) (Cyber Ambassador and former Minister of Digital Affairs, Taiwan), [Beth Simone Noveck](https:/thegovlab.org/beth-simone-noveck.html) (Founder of InnovateUS and Chief AI Strategist, New Jersey), [Danielle Allen](https:/danielleallen.scholars.harvard.edu) (Director of the Allen Lab for Democracy Renovation, Harvard Kennedy School)
 
 This conversation covered the origins of Taiwan's digital democracy infrastructure, the tools and conditions that make public deliberation work, and how to assess whether a given context is suited for online or in-person methods. **Tang's central argument is that democracy breaks down when it operates too slowly.** Democratic institutions designed for 60-day cycles cannot respond to problems that move in minutes. When people participate and see no results, they become cynical; cynicism creates an opening for populism and extremism. **The goal is to make democracy "fast, fair, and fun" so that participation delivers visible outcomes quickly enough to sustain engagement.**
 
 ## The 2014 Sunflower Movement and the origins of vTaiwan
 
 In 2014, Taiwan's president Ma Ying-jeou had a 9% approval rating. His administration was attempting to pass a trade agreement with Beijing, and in the process public trust had collapsed. In March of that year, roughly half a million people occupied Taiwan's legislature for three weeks in what became known as the [Sunflower Movement](https:/mobilisationlab.org/stories/blooming-digital-democracy-taiwan-sunflower-movement) . Tang, then 33, was among the occupiers.
 
 The occupation was organized as a large-scale citizen assembly. Participants formed small groups to deliberate on specific aspects of the trade deal. Tang's group focused on cybersecurity concerns, including reliance on Chinese telecom companies such as Huawei and ZTE. **Each day organizers announced what had been agreed the previous day and what remained to be discussed.** After three weeks the groups had converged on a coherent set of proposals. The Speaker of Parliament accepted them.
 
 Following the occupation, Tang was invited to serve as a " [reverse mentor](https:/govinsider.asia/intl-en/article/could-government-change-permanently-after-covid-19-audrey-tang-taiwan) " to cabinet ministers. **Reverse mentorship is a specific mechanism Taiwan adopted: young people (always under 35) advise senior officials, rather than the other way around.** The idea emerged from observations during the Sunflower Movement that younger generations operate more on horizontal, peer-to-peer trust networks rather than vertical institutional trust. They may respect institutions but do not find them relevant to their lives. Bringing people with horizontal credibility into the cabinet creates incentives for the government to stay connected to those networks. Tang describes the design intention as being "more popular than populism."
 
 Tang's task as a reverse mentor was to replicate the Sunflower deliberation process online so that future controversies (like the emerging fight over Uber regulation) would not require another occupation. The result was [](https:/vtaiwan.tw) [vTaiwan](https:/vtaiwan.tw) . (Also: GovLab write-up on vTaiwan)
 
 ## vTaiwan and Pol.is
 
 [vTaiwan](https:/vtaiwan.tw) is an online platform for public deliberation on policy questions. It launched in 2015 and has been used for issues including Uber regulation, Airbnb rules, online alcohol sales, platform liability for disinformation, fintech sandboxes, and more. The platform uses entirely open-source technology, meaning anyone can inspect and verify the algorithms. [As of 2020 it had 200,000 participants and has led to at least 26 pieces of legislation.](https:/rebootdemocracy.ai/blog/was-vtaiwan-such-a-big-flop-after-all) Since launching, over 80% of vTaiwan deliberations have led to decisive government action.
 
 It is not a government platform. **It exists independently and operates as a collaboration between civil society and public sector.** Specifically, three parties operate it: government agencies that sponsor issues and commit to respond, editors from the Science & Technology Law Institute who translate proposals into digestible formats, and g0v volunteers who maintain the system. This structure benefits from buy-in and legitimacy that a purely government-run platform might lack.
 
 The core tool within vTaiwan is [](https:/pol.is) [Pol.is](https:/pol.is) , an AI-assisted system for large-scale opinion gathering. Pol.is works differently from standard social media or comment sections. Participants see statements submitted by other users and can agree, disagree, or pass. **They cannot reply to statements or share them. This design eliminates the mechanisms that allow trolling and outrage to spread. There is no way to dunk on someone or go viral through provocation.** Further, Poli.s visualizes participants as clusters based on their response patterns. If two people tend to agree and disagree on the same statements, they appear near each other. **The system then identifies "bridging statements": statements that achieve agreement across clusters that otherwise disagree.** These bridging statements surface to the top. The algorithm inverts the usual social media dynamic where divisive content rises. Here, unifying content rises.
 
 Tang calls the goal " **uncommon ground** ": areas of agreement that surprise participants. The experience of discovering that you agree with people you assumed were opponents is what makes participation feel worthwhile. In Tang's framing, it is the "fun" part of democracy.
 
 [The Uber case](https:/blog.pol.is/uber-responds-to-vtaiwans-coherent-blended-volition-3e9b75102b9b) ( [other article too](https:/www.technologyreview.com/2018/08/21/240284/the-simple-but-ingenious-system-taiwan-uses-to-crowdsource-its-laws) ) is a relevant example from Taiwan. In 2015, three government ministries (Transportation, Economy, and Finance) had conflicting positions on how to regulate ride-sharing. **They publicly committed to respond to any proposal that achieved 85% or more support across groups on vTaiwan.** This pre-commitment created legitimacy because participants knew their input would matter if they could find common ground. After three weeks of deliberation, participants converged on a regulatory framework. The uber case drew 31,115 total votes, with 925 participants voting on the [Pol.is](http:/pol.is) survey, 1,875 joining the livestreamed consultation meeting, and over 4,000 crowdsourcing the meeting agenda. The Ministry of Transportation pledged to ratify the consensus reached on [Pol.is](http:/pol.is) . The resulting framework became law. By 2020, President Tsai Ing-wen's approval rating exceeded 71%.
 
 Tang also cites [](https:/www.wethepeople250.org) [We the People 250](https:/www.wethepeople250.org) , a recent U.S. project using similar methods. Run in collaboration with the Napolitan Institute and Google Jigsaw, it gathered 2,000 Americans (five from each congressional district) as a statistical microcosm of the country. Despite participants identifying as conservative or liberal, **97% agreed on statements about values starting at home and judging people by character rather than appearance** . The polarization that dominates media coverage did not show up in the data.
 
 ## Enabling conditions
 
 Generalizing from their work in Taiwan, Tang identifies three requirements for launching public deliberation processes that influence policy:
 
 (1) Air cover. Politicians must pre-commit to respond to results. The Uber case worked because three ministers publicly agreed to act on proposals with 85%+ cross-group support. Physically or legally impossible proposals can still be vetoed. But the commitment creates legitimacy. Participants need to know their input will matter.
 
 (2) Accountability through openness. vTaiwan's algorithms are open source. Participants can independently verify how clustering works and how bridging statements are identified. Tang likens this to [](https:/communitynotes.x.com) [Community Notes](https:/communitynotes.x.com) on X, which uses the same bridging concept and publishes its algorithm and data publicly.
 
 (3) Urgency for clarity. The best use cases involve genuinely unsettled questions where no existing government silo can claim expertise. Uber in 2015 was one example because nobody knew how to regulate ride-sharing. When the problem is new enough that bureaucracies cannot pretend to have answers, there is more room for public input to shape the outcome.
 
 ## Tool selection: discovery vs. definition, and when to go online vs offline
 
 Tang distinguishes between tools for different phases of deliberation, using a double-diamond metaphor. [](https:/pol.is) [Poli.s](https:/pol.is) **is good for the "discover" phase: open-ended exploration of what people think.** You might use it to ask how people feel about the future of their city in 2050, or what concerns them about AI.
 
 [**Ethelo**](https:/ethelo.com) **,** [****](https:/stanforddeliberate.org) [**Stanford Online Deliberation**](https:/stanforddeliberate.org) **, and** [**Frankly**](https:/frankly.org) [****](https:/frankly.org) **work better for the "define" phase: settling on a final package from established options.** Ethelo calculates an "Ethelo score" that favors proposals making everybody slightly unhappy but nobody very unhappy. N This is a proportionate veto approach. The same bridging spirit as Pol . is but expressed through a different mechanism.
 
 Tang emphasizes that these tools are not mutually exclusive. A single deliberation might use Pol.is for initial agenda-setting, then move to Ethelo or Stanford Deliberation to finalize a policy package.
 
 Tang introduces "PPM" (polarization per minute) as a diagnostic for thinking about in-person, online, and hybrid engagement methods. PPM is essentially a metaphorical polarization barometer.
 
 **In low-polarization environments, asynchronous online deliberation works well, says Tang.** Finland has used Pol.is for nationwide deliberations on topics including the future of AI. The most polarizing statement in Finland's Pol.is that data shows older people feeling that younger people correct their word choices too often. If that is your most divisive issue, you have a low-PPM environment.
 
 **In highly polarized environments, like the United States, in-person components become necessary, says Tang.** They describe the U.S. as having "a lot of geothermal energy" because polarization generates heat. In these contexts, people need nonverbal cues and shared physical space to recognize that polarization is partly an illusion. Online-only approaches allow too much psychological projection onto the other side. You need the experience of sitting at a table with someone and discovering you agree.
 
 ## Radical transparency
 
 Tang also practices and encourages what they call "radical transparency." Over the past 10 years, Tang has published full transcripts of all meetings, totaling conversations with 8,000 people across more than 2,000 locations. These are available in the public domain at [](https:/sayit.archive.tw) [sayit.archive.tw](https:/sayit.archive.tw) . Lobbyists, journalists, or anyone else can meet with Tang, but only if they agree to publish the complete transcript afterward.
 
 Two effects follow. **First, lobbyists talk exclusively about public goods because they know people will read the transcript.** When David Plouffe lobbied Tang on behalf of Uber, he spoke only about climate benefits and reduced congestion. He made no arguments that benefited only Uber. **Second, full context cuts through polarization.** Online polarization often relies on taking statements out of context and amplifying the most inflammatory reading. When full transcripts are public, the full context is easier to access than the distortion.
 
 Tang notes that language models trained on this public data now accurately represent their positions. The cost of radical transparency has dropped dramatically with AI handling transcription and publication.
 
 ## Engaged California and polarization on wildfires
 
 Tang has worked with Governor Gavin Newsom and Jennifer Siebel Newsom for several years on [Engaged California](https:/engaged.ca.gov) , a platform for public deliberation. The original focus was youth mental health and social media: how should young people use social media to support their wellbeing? This question invited input from people affected by policy (youth) who cannot vote.
 
 The platform had already been developed when the Los Angeles fires occurred in early 2025. [The team pivoted immediately to wildfire survivors](https:/engaged.ca.gov/lafires-recovery) from the Eaton and Palisades fires, asking how to overcome NIMBYism around fire mitigation and prevention, working to develop a “fire recovery action plan.”
 
 **Traditional polls on this topic showed extreme positions. But when Engaged California placed people in groups of 10 and asked them to react to each other's feelings, they shifted.** Instead of NIMBY (not in my backyard) or YIMBY (yes in my backyard), participants moved to what Tang calls MIMBY: "maybe in my backyard, if you do this, if I do that." A bridging algorithm surfaced proposals to unify groups, [resulting in a comprehensive report on wildfire recovery.](https:/engaged.ca.gov/lafires-recovery/action-plan) California is now using the same platform [for state employees to shape AI adoption in government](https:/engaged.ca.gov/stateemployees) from the bottom up.
 
 ## Starting hyperlocal: Bowling Green, KY
 
 In Bowling Green, Kentucky, organizers ran a project called " [What Could Bowling Green Be?](https:/medium.com/jigsaw/how-one-of-the-fastest-growing-cities-in-kentucky-used-ai-to-plan-for-the-next-25-years-3b70c4fd1412) " that engaged roughly 10% of the local population (about 8,000 people). **They used printed QR codes and door-to-door outreach combined with living room conversations.** Tang mentions this example because it further illustrates the success of engagements with intentional design, which keep in mind the local context and community
 
 **The project worked with a range of "listening partners":** the Boys and Girls Club, housing groups, public health organizations, faith communities, storytelling groups, and others. Each partner had their own way of convening people (food, sports, spirituality, etc.), but all fed into a shared Pol.is conversation.
 
 Pol.is now uses language models to auto-generate topic labels (community identity, equity and inclusion, infrastructure, transportation, etc.), eliminating the need for manual coding. Tang describes the output as an "evolving group selfie" that becomes a "selfie movie" as participation continues over time.
 
 ## Pre-bunking instead of debunking
 
 Polarization is deeply connected to how debates and discourse develop, especially in online environments. **Tang says that reframing issues intentionally (pre-bunking) can be an effective tool against misinformation and polarization.**
 
 Taiwan is the world's top target for foreign information interference, according to [](https:/v-dem.net) [V-Dem data](https:/v-dem.net) (12 years running). Tang notes that Taiwan gets "free penetration testing" from hostile actors. **One lesson Tang shares: in saturated information environments, debunking does not work and can backfire by reinforcing the frame of the attack.**
 
 **Pre-bunking works differently. Before polarizing narratives take hold, you release something more viral that reframes the issue.** During COVID, two competing mask narratives emerged in Taiwan. One claimed only N95 masks work and everything else is placebo. The other claimed masks cause harm and N95s are dangerous. Rather than debunk either, [the government released a meme featuring a Shiba Inu (the "spokesdog") with her paw over her mouth, captioned: masks remind you to keep unwashed hands from your face.](https:/www.taipeitimes.com/News/taiwan/archives/2020/02/18/2003731193)
 
 The cute dog went more viral than either disinformation strain. Handwashing rates increased. The mask debate became associated with a friendly reminder instead of tribal conflict. The pre-bunk had set the frame before polarization could take hold.
 
 ## Takeaways for learners
 
 Assess PPM before choosing methods. High-polarization contexts need in-person components. Low-polarization contexts can work asynchronously online. This is a diagnostic, not a rule.
 
 The goal is uncommon ground, not necessarily consensus. The aim is surfacing agreement that is useful and surprising. This discovery is what makes participation rewarding.
 
 Pre-commitment creates legitimacy. Politicians must agree to respond before deliberation starts. Without this, participants have no reason to believe their input matters.
 
 Match tools to phases. Pol.is for divergent discovery, Ethelo or Stanford Deliberation for convergent definition. Know which phase you are in.
 
 Pre-bunking beats debunking. The window to set a frame is narrow. Speed and creativity matter more than having the best counterargument.
 
 Start with the human practice. Active listening at a personal scale is the foundation. The tools are just ways of scaling what you already know how to do one-on-one.

 ## Audience notes
 
 ### Questions
 
 Akinori Oyama (Japan): Asked about the relationship between tech-based and in-real-life engagement, noting studies from MIT that indicate in-person interaction earns more trust. This led to Tang's PPM framework explanation.
 
 Kassondra Wilbur (Maine): "How did you manage the need for transparency with competing priorities for confidentiality and flooding the zone with too much information that it causes confusion for the citizenry?" This led to the pre-bunking discussion.
 
 Charles Pfeffer (Maine): "What's the smallest scale example you have for applying pro-social technology approaches?" This led to Tang's answer about active listening at a scale of one.
 
 Sonia Putzel (NYC Civic Engagement Commission): Asked about what motivates first-time engagement and whether keeping people engaged is different. Tang answered about people loving to set the agenda and being experts in their own feelings.
 
 Stephen Buckley: Asked about standard exit surveys to evaluate citizen experience. Tang confirmed they use them and explained the "can you live with it" question for the 15% who didn't get their preferred outcome.
 
 ### Questions raised in chat but not directly answered
 
 Kassondra Wilbur: "Democracy does require a lot more effort than most other governing structures, how did you convince citizens that it is worth the gargantuan amount of effort to get to a single decision point?"
 
 K Sherwin: "Does anyone have experience convincing their political leaders (e.g. Ministers) to be on board with this approach?" (seeking peer connections on air cover)
 
 Kassondra Wilbur: "Does anyone else experience extreme silos between executive leadership and the remainder of the employees in the org?"
 
 ### Polling and locations
 
 Zoom polling showed participants' reasons for attending:
 
 (1) learning about new AI tools for engagement (59%)
 
 (2) increasing confidence in facilitating engagement (52%)
 
 (3) building confidence in applying platforms for public value (48%)
 
 (4) and learning new skills or techniques (48%)
 
 Top challenges cited:
 
 (1) lack of time or staff capacity (44%)
 
 (2) difficulty reaching diverse audiences (30%)
 
 (3) limited technical skills (26%)
 
 (4) limited organizational support (26%)
 
 (5) and low public trust (26%)
 
 Participants joined from:
 
 California (Caltrans, California Office of Data and Innovation, California High-Speed Rail Authority), New Jersey (Civil Service Commission, State Employment & Training Commission), Delaware, Iowa, Oregon, Maine, Georgia, Kentucky (InnoEngine in Bowling Green), Arizona, New York City (Civic Engagement Commission), Washington DC, Japan, Chile, Mexico (Digital Agency of Baja California), Canada (British Columbia), Spain (Pompeu Fabra University in Barcelona), and Sweden.
 
 ## Quotes
 
 ### Audrey Tang (Cyber Ambassador, Taiwan)
 
 "I think it is a core pathology for people to treat democracy like a finished building rather than a piece of storytelling, a piece of software."
 
 "If we fix the latency problem so that people can get democracy delivering results here and now, I think that democracy can be fast, fair, and fun again."
 
 "People really love the ability to set the agenda... People are really experts in their own feelings."
 
 "In a place with very advanced PPM situation, a lot of geothermal energy, as I like to say, because polarization brings energy, you do need this kind of lived experience so that people can check using nonverbal expressions."
 
 "The reverse mentorship is a design, back in 2014, to be more popular than populism."
 
 ### Danielle Allen (Allen Lab, Harvard)
 
 "It turns out that fairness is fun, actually, that the kind of thing that brings us common
 
 ground, makes that visible, is fun and rewarding."
 
 "Every technical solution is actually just a way of concretizing a human practice. What matters most is the human practice."
 
 ### Beth Simone Noveck (InnovateUS, New Jersey)
 
 "I think the thing that we've also heard very clearly is that it's really not about the tools in the end. It is about the trust in people and their ideas, their experience, that active listening."
 
 "The best places have been doing this kind of listening for some time... It doesn't take AI, it's about process."
